1#main: The laws of kilay hakerem and kilay zera'im. In it are 69 seifim. One who sows two species of grain or two species of vegetables together with vineyard seed—behold he receives lashes twice: once for "your field you shall not sow kilayim," and once for "you shall not sow your vineyard kilayim." And he does not receive lashes for "you shall not sow your vineyard kilayim" until he sows in Eretz Yisrael wheat, barley, and vine seed casually (mefolut yad). And likewise if he covered them with earth he receives lashes. And likewise if he sowed two species of vegetables and vine seed, or one species of vegetable and one species of grain and vine seed casually—behold he receives lashes. And he is liable d'oraisa only for hemp, luf, and similar seeds that complete their growth together with vineyard grain; but other seeds are forbidden by rabbinic decree. And likewise it is forbidden by rabbinic decree to sow kilay hakerem in the Diaspora. And one does not plow with a non-Jew in kilayim, but one uproots with him in order to lessen the loss.
2#main: It is forbidden only because of kilay hakerem for species of grain and species of vegetables alone; but other species of seeds are permitted to sow them in a vineyard, and needless to say other trees.
3#main: It is forbidden to sow vegetables or grain beside the vines, or to plant a vine beside the vegetable or the grain; and if he did so, even though he does not receive lashes, behold he has caused hikdish and both are forbidden in benefit—the vegetable or grain and the vines—and one burns both of them, as it says, "lest the fullness of the seed be hallowed." And even the straw of the grain and the wood of these vines are forbidden in benefit and one burns them, and one does not kindle an oven or stove with them nor cook with them at the time of their burning.
4#main: Whether one plants or one maintains—once he saw kilayim grew in his vineyard and left them, behold he has caused hikdish. And a person does not cause hikdish something that is not his. Therefore one who roofs his vine over his friend's grain has caused hikdish to his vine and the grain was not hallowed; one who roofs his friend's vine over his grain has caused hikdish to his grain and did not cause hikdish to his friend's vine; one who roofs his friend's vine over his friend's grain—neither caused hikdish. And for this reason one who sows his vineyard in the shemittah year did not cause hikdish.
5#main: One who sees kilayim in his friend's vineyard and maintains them—behold the seer is forbidden in their benefit and every person is permitted in them. But if the owner of the vineyard maintained them, he would cause them to be hallowed for every person, as we explained.
6#main: A coerced person who sowed kilayim in his friend's vineyard—if the owners were asleep, even though they did not despair, behold he has caused hikdish d'oraisa. And if the owners were not asleep, even though they despaired, he does not cause hikdish except by rabbinic decree.
7#main: Wind that uprooted clusters of the vine and sent them onto the grain—he must fence them off immediately. And if coercion occurred and he did not remove them, behold these are permitted and were not hallowed.
8#main: A coerced person who sowed the vineyard—when the coercion ends he must harvest the seed immediately, even on the weekday of a festival. And if he did not find workers he adds up to a third to their wages; if they asked him for more or he did not find workers, behold he asks calmly and harvests. And if the seed was delayed until the season when it causes hikdish, behold he has caused hikdish and both are forbidden.
9#main: From when are grain or vegetables hallowed? From when they take root. And grapes—from when they form the white double leaf.
10#main: A vineyard whose grapes have not reached forming the white double leaf but are still unripe (boser), and seed was sown within vegetable or grain and took root—this has not caused hikdish; nevertheless we penalize him and forbid the seed, but the unripe grapes are permitted. And if he uprooted the seed before the grapes formed the white double leaf, behold it is permitted in benefit. If part formed the white double leaf and part did not—those that formed were hallowed, and those that did not are permitted.
11#main: Grapes that formed the white double leaf and seed was sown beside them—grain or vegetable species—and he harvested the seed before it took root, behold it is permitted in benefit; and if it took root, it is forbidden.
12#main: A vine whose leaves dried and fell as a vine dries in days of cold—it is forbidden to sow vegetable or grain beside it; and if he sowed, he did not cause hikdish. And likewise one who sows in an unperforated pot placed in a vineyard did not cause hikdish, and we give him lashes of rebellion. But a perforated pot—behold it is like the ground.
13#main: If he was working in a vineyard and seeds fell from him, or came out with manure or with water, or he was sowing or winnowing in a white field and the wind blew them behind him and the seeds fell in the vineyard and grew—behold this was not hallowed, as it says, "that you sow"—and this he did not sow. And he is liable to uproot when he sees; and if he maintained them, behold he has caused hikdish. And if the wind blew them before him and he saw the seeds that fell to the vineyard, behold this is like one who sows. And how should he act? If grasses grew, he turns them with a plowshare and that suffices; and if he found them become ears, he beats that ear in order to ruin it, for everything is forbidden in benefit; and if he found them become grain, behold he burns it. And if he saw them and maintained them, behold these are burned with the vines adjacent to them.
14#main: One who sees in a vineyard a grass that people do not customarily sow, even though he wants to maintain it for an animal or for medicine—behold he has not caused hikdish until he maintains something that the majority of people in that place maintain similarly. How so? One who maintains thorns in a vineyard in the evening when they want thorns for their camels—behold he has caused hikdish. Iris, cassia, and royal rose—and other seed species are not kilayim in a vineyard. Kundos and cotton vine—behold they are like other vegetable species and cause hikdish in a vineyard. And likewise all types of grasses that grow on their own in a field—behold they cause hikdish in a vineyard. And Egyptian beans are a seed species and do not cause hikdish.
15#main: Reeds, rose, and myrtle (meaning: a type of myrtle in Aruch)—are tree species and are not kilayim in a vineyard. This is the rule: whatever produces leaves from its trunk—behold it is a vegetable; and whatever does not produce leaves from its trunk—behold it is a tree. And caper is a tree for every matter.
16#main: One who sees vegetable in a vineyard and says, when I reach it I will harvest it—it is permitted; he reached it and passed over it and said, when I return to it I will harvest it—if he waited until it increased one part in one hundred, behold he has caused hikdish.
17#main: It is forbidden to pass by a perforated pot in which vegetable is sown inside a vineyard; and if he placed it under the vine and it remained there in the ground long enough to add one in two hundred, behold it has caused hikdish.
18#main: Onion that was planted in a vineyard and afterward the vineyard was uprooted, and afterward onions grew from the planted root—even though the growths exceeded its root by two hundred, behold that root remains in its prohibition, for permitted growths do not elevate the forbidden root.
19#main: One who sows grain or vegetable in a vineyard, or maintains it, until it increased by one in two hundred—behold he causes hikdish from the vines around it sixteen amot in every direction, circular—not square—and we view the whole circle whose width is thirty-two amot as though it were entirely full of vegetable, and every vine that is within this circle is hallowed with the vegetable; and whatever is outside the circle is not hallowed.
20#main: In what case is this said? When between the edges of this circle and the rows of vines beyond it there were more than four amot. But if between them there were four amot precisely or less, we view the circle as though it reached the adjacent row, and as though the width of the circle were forty amot, and we view every vine that falls within this circle of forty amot—behold it is hallowed.
21#main: In what case is this said? When one sows or maintains inside the vineyard; but when one sows outside the vineyard and adjoins it, behold he causes hikdish to two rows of vines adjacent to the seed—meaning, along the entire length of the seed—and another four amot outside the seed; and it is hallowed from the seed a width of four amot along the entire row of the vineyard. And if he sowed beside a single vine, he does not cause hikdish from the seed except six handbreadths in every direction.
22#main: A shoot less than a handbreadth does not cause hikdish to seeds. In what case is this said? With two corresponding to two and one protruding a tail; but if the whole vineyard is so, behold it causes hikdish.
23#main: Two gardens one above the other—the lower is made a vineyard: he sows the upper until it reaches the airspace of ten handbreadths near the vineyard, for an airspace of ten handbreadths is adjacent to a vineyard or a single vine, and it is forbidden to sow seeds in it. And if the upper was made a vineyard, behold he sows the lower until it reaches below three handbreadths from the root of the vines.
24#main: One whose field was sown with vegetable or grain and he reconsidered to plant vines in it—he turns over the seeds with a plowshare and afterward plants, and he does not plant and afterward turn over.
25#main: If it was planted with vines and he reconsidered to sow seeds in it—he uproots the vines and afterward sows the seeds. And if he wished to prune the vines until less than a handbreadth remains near the ground, behold it is permitted to sow, and afterward he returns and uproots what remains of the vines in the ground.
26#main: One who layered three vines and their roots are visible—if between them there are from four amot up to eight, behold they combine with other standing vines as though he had not layered them; and if not, they do not combine. If there were fewer than three, they do not combine except that he distances from them six handbreadths in every direction and sows.
27#main: Whatever one sows under the tendrils and leaves emerging from the vine—behold he has caused hikdish, even though the seed is far from the root of the vine many amot. One who suspends the vine on part of a trellis (meaning: woven wood or reeds on which vine tendrils are suspended when very long)—he may not sow under the permitted part of the trellis, even though there are no leaves or tendrils on them; and if he sowed, since the seed is not under the vine's covering, behold it is permitted. And likewise if he suspended the vine on part of the beams of a tree that does not produce fruit, such as cedar and cypress. But if he suspended on part of a food tree, behold it is permitted to sow under the beams of the tree on which vine tendrils did not spread, for a person does not cancel a food tree and make it a trellis for a vine; and if tendrils spread after he sowed and covered the seed, behold he returns them elsewhere.
28#main: One who sowed under the permitted part of the trellis or under the permitted part of a tree that does not produce fruit, and vine tendrils spread and covered the seeds—behold it is forbidden to maintain them or to return the tendrils; rather how does he act? He uproots the seed.
29#main: Reeds emerging from the trellis (meaning: the wood or reeds on which the vine is supported) and he spared cutting them so as not to ruin the trellis—behold it is permitted to sow beneath them; and if he left them so that tendrils and leaves emerging would walk upon them, behold it is forbidden to sow beneath them.
30#main: A branch emerging from the trellis or from the single vine trained on stakes—we view it as though a weight were hanging from it to the ground, and it is forbidden to sow beneath it. And likewise one who stretches a vine branch from tree to tree—it is forbidden to sow beneath it. If he tied a rope or reed to the vine branch and tied the other end to a tree, behold it is permitted to sow beneath the rope; and if he stretched this rope so that tendrils and leaves would walk upon it, behold it is like a trellis and forbidden to sow beneath it.
31#main: One who comes to sow beside the vineyard distances four amot from the roots of the vines and sows. And if it is a single vine, he distances six handbreadths from it and sows.
32#main: If there was one row of vines one beside the other, even if there are a hundred, this is not a vineyard but like a single vine, and he distances six handbreadths from the row and sows. If there were two rows, behold this is a vineyard and he must distance four amot on every side and afterward sow. And how many must be in each row? Three vines or more. In what case is this said? When between each vine and vine there were from four amot up to eight; but if between the two rows there were eight amot apart from the place of the vines, behold these are like separated one from the other and are not one vineyard, and he distances only six handbreadths from each row. And likewise if between them there were less than four, behold these are like one vine and he distances six handbreadths in every direction.
33#main: If there were three rows, even though between them there is less than four, behold these are a vineyard and we view the middle ones as though they are not.
34#main: If there were three rows and between each row and row eight amot or more, behold he sows between the rows; therefore one who plants his vineyard at the outset and distances between each row and row eight amot may bring seed into it and distances from each row and row only six handbreadths. But if he sowed outside it, he must distance from the outer row four amot like other vineyards, and the law between the rows of this vineyard is not like a vineyard ruined in its middle, for from the outset they were planted distant.
35#main: If in this field there was one row of vines and in his friend's field another row opposite it near to it—even though a private path or public path or a fence lower than ten handbreadths separates between them—behold they combine to become both a vineyard, provided between them there is less than eight.
